# General — cross-strategy material

## Rules & Edits (from the guide)
## Editing a trade — one change, one reason
The dialog keeps reward-to-risk locked: edit one level, the other follows, size re-computes. Three legitimate edits exist. Anything more = the setup is bad, skip it.
| Edit | When | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Widen the stop** | The proposed stop sits just _inside_ an obvious level or round number where a stab is likely | Move it just **beyond** the structure and accept the smaller size. Your data agrees: structural widens have paid; tiny "comfort" widens (≤10 pips) are 0-for-6 — either clear the level or leave it alone. |
| **Pull the target closer** | A major level or round number sits just _before_ the proposed target | Take profit in front of the wall. But: your TP pulls are 0-for-2 so far (see Lessons) — only do this for a concrete visible obstacle, never for comfort, and never replace a bank-half-and-run plan with one near target. |
| **Improve the entry** (pending orders) | A better fill is likely and you accept possibly missing the trade | A better entry that never fills costs 0. Never chase after it misses. |
**Never:** risk above 1% · tighten the stop to buy more size · stretch the target on a feeling · more than one edit per trade.

## Judging any trigger candle — 3 questions
| Pattern | Means | Good version |
|---|---|---|
| **Engulfing** | One side overwhelmed the other in a single bar | Big body, closes near its extreme, swallows several bars — not one doji |
| **Hammer / pin** | A level was stabbed and rejected | The wick actually pierced the level, then snapped back; close in the far third |
| **Full-body drive** | Conviction — this is what a real "shift" looks like | Tiny wicks, often leaves a gap; its absence on an SMC shift = skip |
| **Doji** | Indecision where you needed conviction | There isn't one — a doji trigger is the market shrugging → lean skip |
For any candle: **where** did it print (at a level, or mid-air)? **how big** is it vs. the last 20 bars? **where did it close** in its own range?

## Correlated families — one bet, not several
| Family | Members | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| USD block | every USD pair; gold & indices move inversely | Long EURUSD + long GBPUSD + short USDCHF ≈ 3× one short-dollar bet |
| EUR crosses | EURUSD, EURGBP, EURJPY, EURAUD… | share the EUR leg |
| JPY crosses | USDJPY, EURJPY, GBPJPY, AUDJPY… | risk mood moves them together, violently |
| Risk-on block | AUD, NZD, indices; CHF/JPY inverse | index long + AUDJPY long = one bet |
| Metals | XAUUSD, XAGUSD | silver is gold with leverage |
**Caps:** FTMO hard limits — daily loss 5% ($1,250), total 10% ($2,500); five straight 1% losers in a day breaches. System: ≤3% open+armed at once. Yours: one family = one idea = max 2%.

## Reading the event lines
| Situation | Do |
|---|---|
| High-impact event ahead, within ~12h | **Skip or wait.** A swing entry hours before CPI is a coin flip. |
| Minor event ahead | Trade normally. |
| Recent event behind, bias arrow _agrees_ with you | Mild plus. |
| Recent event behind, bias arrow _against_ you | You're fading fresh fundamentals — demand an A-grade chart. |
| Setup created by the event candle itself | Lean skip — post-news moves extend and reverse violently. |
| Indices / gold / oil | USD events are your events. |

## Jargon → your chart
| Term you'll hear | On your chart |
|---|---|
| Liquidity / stop hunt | the labelled pool lines and the sweep through them |
| Buy-side / sell-side liquidity | pools above price / below price (targets) |
| MSS / CHoCH | the "MSS ✓" break of the last small swing |
| Displacement | the big-bodied leg that makes the shift believable |
| Fair value gap / imbalance | the shaded 3-bar gap boxes |
| Order block | the shaded entry-zone rectangle |
| Premium / discount / OTE | the fib grid; the shaded 61.8–78.6 band is the discount zone |
| Kill zones | bar time in UTC: London 07–13, NY 13–20 — sweeps there mean more than overnight ones |

# Chart-Reading Protocol

The fixed sequence for reading any screenshot. Work top-down; each step constrains the next.
Skipping ahead to "does the candle look good?" is how bad verdicts happen — location and
regime kill more trades than triggers do.

## 0. Inventory — what am I actually looking at?

- Which timeframes were provided? (Ideal: D1 context + H4 setup. H4 alone → verdict is
  provisional; say so and request the D1.)
- What did the trader state? (strategy fired, proposed entry/SL/TP, session, cluster exposure)
- What does the overlay already show? (pool labels, MSS marker, fib grid, zones, event lines,
  R:R readout — the detector's work; don't redo it, judge it)

## 1. Regime — what kind of market is this? (D1)

Classify the visible D1 window (see `mean-reversion-and-regime.md`):
- **Trend**: stairstepping swings one direction, shallow pullbacks, moving average sloped and
  respected.
- **Range**: horizontal boundaries touched repeatedly, flat MA, alternating swings.
- **Volatile/news-driven**: huge bars both directions, overlap, gaps.
- **Transition**: a fresh structure break against the prior regime.

Then apply the quick reference's regime table: the regime alone puts each strategy at a
default lean (e.g., EMA reversion in a clean trend → default SKIP before looking further).

## 2. Structure — map the swings

On the setup timeframe: mark the last 3–4 meaningful swing highs/lows. HH/HL = up, LH/LL =
down, mixed = range. Note *unbroken* levels — untouched swing points are future magnets
(liquidity). Ask: where is the nearest pool above and below price? (`smc-ict-concepts.md`)

## 3. Location — does this spot matter?

The single most predictive question: **is the setup at a level that matters, or floating
mid-range?**
- At/near: prior swing extremes, equal highs/lows, big round numbers, zone/level confluence
  across both timeframes, the origin of a strong prior leg.
- Mid-range, mid-air, far from anything → the setup needs to be exceptional elsewhere,
  and usually isn't. Location failure is a near-automatic SKIP.

## 4. Setup quality — grade what the detector can't

Strategy-specific (use the matching library note + quick-reference flags):
- **SMC**: sweep character (one violent wick vs. grinding chop), displacement force on the
  shift, zone freshness, pool quality.
- **Deep Fib**: impulse leg organic vs. climactic; retracement corrective (slow, overlapping)
  vs. impulsive; band confluence with old structure; trap liquidity just beyond the stop.
- **EMA reversion**: does the chart *look* like a freight train regardless of the numbers;
  consecutive wide directional bars into the extreme; gap-created stretch.
- **Candles**: only score the trigger candle *at the level* — quality tells in
  `candlestick-patterns.md`.

## 5. Risk geometry — is the trade well-shaped?

- SL: is it beyond the *thesis-invalidating* point, or just beyond a number? Is obvious
  liquidity (equal lows/highs, round number) sitting *between* entry and SL that will be
  swept first?
- TP: is there an obstacle (untouched level, round number) *in front of* the target that
  price must chew through? Target behind a wall → ADJUST candidate (pull TP in front).
- Path: does price have room to move, or is the trade fighting structure the whole way?

## 6. Timing overlays

- Session stated by the trader: London/NY moves carry conviction; Asia-session signals on
  FX are weaker (`multi-timeframe-analysis.md`).
- Friday-late entries: weekend gap risk on a multi-day hold — lean SKIP.
- Event lines visible on the overlay near-future → the news rules in the quick reference.

## 7. Verdict — assemble, don't average

- Count decisive factors, not total flags: one disqualifier (location failure, regime
  mismatch, red-folder window) outweighs three mild positives.
- TAKE requires: regime fit + real location + acceptable setup quality + clean geometry.
- ADJUST only for one surgical edit that fixes the *single* flaw in an otherwise-TAKE setup.
- Everything else is SKIP — and "the checklist is mixed and I'm not sure" **is a SKIP**,
  stated as such with low confidence. A missed trade costs 0 R.

Output using the format in CLAUDE.md. Always include "would change my mind."

# Multi-Timeframe Analysis — D1 Context, H4 Trigger

*Distilled from: standard MTF doctrine (Babypips-lineage), ICT killzone concept (timing only),
and this system's D1/H4 convention. Session times in UTC as the system uses them.*

## The principle

Higher timeframe sets the **context** (where price is going and where it matters); lower
timeframe supplies the **trigger** (a precise, well-defined entry within that context). All
of this system's detectors follow D1-context → H4-trigger. The advisor's job splits the same
way: most verdict-changing information is on the D1 shot; most entry-quality information is
on the H4 shot.

## Reading the pair of screenshots

**D1 first, always:**
- Regime (trend/range/volatile/transition — `mean-reversion-and-regime.md`)
- Where is price in the D1 structure? Mid-leg, at a D1 level, at the range extreme?
- What D1 levels sit near the H4 setup's entry, stop, and target? A "clean" H4 trade whose
  TP is 20 pips below a D1 swing high is not clean.

**Then H4:**
- Setup mechanics and trigger quality (the strategy-specific notes)
- Whether H4 structure agrees with the D1 read or is fighting it

## Alignment grades

- **Aligned** (H4 setup trades in the D1 direction / at a D1 level): full-quality setup.
- **Neutral** (D1 rangebound, H4 setup inside it): acceptable — location within the D1 range
  becomes the deciding factor (extremes good, middle bad).
- **Opposed** (H4 setup against a clean D1 trend): the system flags these as counter-trend.
  Default lean SKIP; credible only when the setup sits at a *major* D1 level (the kind that
  ends legs) with an exceptional trigger — and even then, expect a reduced target (counter-
  trend moves die at the first opposing pool).

**Timeframe conflict is not a tiebreak situation** — the higher timeframe owns the trend;
the lower timeframe only ever earns a *countertrend scalp's* worth of confidence against it,
and this system swings, not scalps.

## Session timing (UTC)

- **Asia (~00–07)**: thin FX participation; ranges, drifts, and false moves. Signals printed
  here carry less conviction — a sweep with nobody at the desk swept few real stops.
- **London (~07–13)**: first real liquidity; the day's initial directional push; London
  often *creates* the day's extreme — sweeps of overnight/Asia levels here are meaningful.
- **New York (~13–20)**: full liquidity (overlap with London until ~16), most scheduled
  news; late NY fades into thin closing hours.
- Practical weighting: London/NY-session signals > Asia signals, especially for SMC sweeps.
  The trader supplies session (never the date); if not stated, ask for session only.

## Calendar structure without dates

Blindness forbids dates, not day-of-week/session logic:
- **Late-Friday entries**: a multi-day H4 swing hold across a weekend gap is uncompensated
  risk — lean SKIP (the quick reference lists it as an always-skip).
- **Monday opens**: gap artifacts and unfilled weekend moves distort structure briefly.
- **Visible event lines** on the overlay: apply the quick reference's news rules (red-folder
  within ~12h → skip/wait; setup created *by* an event candle → distrust).

## H4-specific caveats (this system's granularity)

- H4 bars cut at fixed UTC boundaries (00/04/08/12/16/20) — "session" reads are approximate
  by whole bars; don't over-interpret which session a single bar belongs to.
- One H4 bar can contain an entire news event: a strange, huge H4 bar mid-chart often *is*
  a release. Treat its extremes as event artifacts, not structure, when grading levels.

## What this means for a verdict

- No D1 shot → provisional verdict, say so, request it. The D1 is where most SKIPs live.
- Name the alignment grade explicitly in every verdict (aligned / neutral / opposed).
- Weight trigger conviction by session; discount Asia-hour signals.
- Apply Friday/weekend and event-line rules mechanically — they're cheap to check and they
  veto everything else.

# Candlestick Patterns — Context Only

*Distilled from: Steve Nison, "Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques" (concept lineage);
StockCharts ChartSchool intro + bullish/bearish reversal pages (full copies in `full-texts/`);
Wikipedia (candlestick pattern/chart). Filtered to what matters on closed D1/H4 bars.*

## The iron rule

**A candlestick pattern has no meaning except at a location that matters.** A perfect
engulfing mid-range is decoration. The same engulfing at a swept pool, a discount zone, or a
stretch extreme is evidence. Score location first (protocol step 3); only then grade the candle.

Corollary: patterns are **closed-bar** objects. A "beautiful hammer" that hasn't closed yet
is a rumor.

## The patterns that matter here (and their quality tells)

### Engulfing (the strongest single-bar reversal evidence)
Body engulfs the prior bar's body, closing opposite to the prior move.
- **Strong**: large body, closes in the top/bottom 10–20% of its range, engulfs *several*
  prior bars, appears after an extended move into a level.
- **Weak**: barely covers a doji; long wick against the close direction; prints in chop.

### Pin bar / hammer / shooting star (rejection)
Long wick (≥1.5–2× body) probing a level, close back in the far third of the range.
- **Strong**: the wick *pierces* the level in question and snaps back — that's the rejection.
- **Weak**: the wick never reached the level ("rejection" of nothing); or the whole bar is
  tiny relative to recent bars (no participation).

### Marubozu / displacement candle (conviction, not reversal)
Full body, minimal wicks. Not an entry pattern — it's *evidence about the leg it belongs to*:
a structure break on a marubozu is a real shift; a break on small overlapping bars is drift.
Consecutive marubozu *against* a mean-reversion idea = momentum, don't fade it.

### Doji / spinning top (indecision)
Tiny body, wicks both ways. At a level where the setup *needs conviction*, a doji trigger is
the market shrugging — downgrade the setup. A doji is only meaningful as the *first* pause
after a strong leg (potential exhaustion), and even then it needs the next bar to confirm.

### Inside bar (compression)
Whole bar inside the prior bar's range. At a decision level after a strong leg: coiling before
continuation. As a standalone "trigger": hesitation, not a signal. Never an entry pattern in
this system.

### Two/three-bar combinations (morning/evening star, three soldiers)
All reduce to the same logic: move into a level → indecision → committed reversal bar. Read
them as that sequence rather than memorizing names — the committed third bar is the trigger,
and its quality tells are the engulfing tells above.

## Reading any candle: three questions

1. **Where** did it print? (at a level = signal; mid-air = noise)
2. **What's its size** relative to the last ~20 bars? (participation — a signal candle should
   be at least average-sized; tiny patterns are tiny evidence)
3. **Where did it close** within its own range? (closes near the extreme = conviction;
   mid-range close = the fight isn't over)

## Common traps

- **Pattern-hunting**: scanning until some bar matches a name. The setup selects the candle,
  never the reverse.
- **Wick-worship**: long wicks *into* a trend direction are often continuation refueling, not
  reversal ("stop-run then go").
- **News candles**: a giant engulfing printed by a scheduled release obeys event dynamics,
  not pattern statistics — see the quick reference's econ rules.
- **Counting patterns in chop**: in overlapping ranges every other bar "is" a pattern.
  If the last 10 bars contain 4 named patterns, the answer is regime, not candles.

## What this means for a verdict

- The trigger candle can *confirm* a setup or *downgrade* it; it can never rescue a bad
  location or wrong regime.
- Grade the trigger with the three questions; quote the answer in the verdict ("engulfing is
  large, closes on its high, at the zone — quality trigger").
- A doji or undersized trigger where the spec wanted an engulf/pin = one concrete reason to
  lean SKIP.

# Risk & Trade Management — R-Multiples, Expectancy, Edits

*Distilled from: Van Tharp's R-multiple/expectancy framework ("Trade Your Way to Financial
Freedom" lineage); FTMO's published account rules; this system's specs. The advisor reasons
in R, never in dollars.*

## Think in R

**1 R = the amount risked** (here: 1% of the account, ~$250, already exact — the system sizes
every trade so entry→SL = 1 R). Every outcome is a multiple: a win to a 3R target = +3 R,
a full stop = −1 R. This normalizes across symbols, volatility, and lot sizes; it is the only
honest scoreboard.

**Expectancy** = (win% × avg win in R) − (loss% × avg loss in R). Two consequences the advisor
must carry into every verdict:
- **Win rate alone is meaningless.** A 40%-WR system at 3R average wins is excellent
  (0.4×3 − 0.6×1 = +0.6 R/trade); a 60%-WR system at 0.8R wins is near-worthless after costs.
- Each of this system's strategies has its own profile (SMC ~40–45% at 2.5–4R; Fib ~45–50% at
  2.5–5R; EMA ~55–62% at 1.3–2R). **Losing streaks are arithmetic, not evidence**: at 45% WR,
  five straight losses happen routinely. Never let recent outcomes shade a verdict on the
  next chart — that's the trader's tilt imported into the advisor.

## Geometry standards for a verdict

- The stop belongs beyond the **thesis-invalidation point** (sweep extreme, deep-fib break,
  stretch extreme) — not at a distance chosen to feel comfortable. If invalidation is too far
  for the size floor, the correct answer is no trade, never a tighter arbitrary stop.
- The R:R quoted by the dialog is real only if the target is *reachable*: a 3R target behind
  two untouched pools and a round number is nominal, not expected.
- Between entry and stop, look for **trap liquidity** (equal extremes, round numbers): stops
  positioned just beyond an obvious magnet get swept-then-reversed. Stop placement quality is
  the most common legitimate ADJUST.

## The surgical-edit doctrine (mirrors the quick reference)

At most **one** edit per trade, each with exactly one justification:
1. **Widen SL** behind clearer structure — when the proposed stop sits just inside an obvious
   level/number. Size shrinks to hold 1%; that's correct, not a cost.
   **Never the reverse**: tightening a stop into structure to buy lots converts a good trade
   into a coin flip and breaks the 1%-risk logic.
2. **Pull TP in front of an obstacle** — sacrifice a fraction of R to stand in front of the
   wall instead of behind it.
3. **Improve entry** (pending) — only when missing the fill entirely is acceptable. A better
   entry that never fills costs 0 R; chasing after a cancelled improvement is the real loss.

Needs two edits → the setup is being redesigned, not adjusted → SKIP.

## Portfolio context (cluster risk)

Correlated positions are **one bet at summed risk**: two same-direction USD-pair trades ≈ 2%
on a single idea. The trader reports exposure in cluster terms; the advisor's rule:
- Same-cluster same-direction position already open → the new setup must be *better* than
  the open one to justify doubling the idea — usually it isn't → lean SKIP.
- System caps (context, not advisor-enforced): ≤3% concurrent open+armed risk; FTMO hard
  limits 5% daily / 10% max. At 1% per trade the limits are generous *unless* correlation
  makes three trades secretly one.

## Management principles (for "should I have moved my stop"-type questions)

- The stop moves only when the *thesis* improves (e.g., to break-even after the first target
  banks — the system does this automatically), never because of discomfort.
- Scale-outs trade expectancy for variance reduction — banking half at TP1 lowers the average
  win but raises consistency; that's the system's deliberate design, don't advise overriding
  it ad hoc.
- Time-stops are legitimate: a thesis that hasn't begun working after several bars (the
  system's expiry windows) is weaker than one that never triggered.

## What this means for a verdict

- Express everything in R; never in dollars or pips.
- Judge stop placement against invalidation + trap liquidity; judge targets against
  reachability; propose at most one surgical edit.
- Fold cluster exposure into the verdict when reported.
- Refuse recency logic — the last trade's outcome has zero bearing on this chart.
